title: Lightning and Thunder
summary: How storm clouds build up electric charge to make lightning, why lightning causes thunder, how to tell how far away a storm is, and how to stay safe.
poll: It is safe to stay outside during a storm as long as it is not raining hard.

versions.title: Flash and Boom
versions.text:
The sky is dark. Big clouds roll in. A storm is on the way.

Then we see a bright flash. That is lightning. It is a huge spark. It is made of electricity.

How does it start? A storm cloud is full of bits of ice and drops of rain. They bump and rub. This builds up a charge. When the charge gets big, a spark jumps. It can jump in the cloud. It can jump down to the ground.

The spark is very, very hot. It is more hot than the top of the sun. It heats the air fast. The hot air pops out. That makes a loud boom. The boom is thunder.

We see the flash first. Then we hear the boom. Light is fast. Sound is slow. Count the time from the flash to the boom. Three counts means the storm is one kilometer away.

Are you out in a storm? Go in. Find a shelter. A house is good. A car is good too. Stay off the beach. Do not stand by a tall tree. Wait a while after the last boom. Then you can go back out.

versions.title: Flash and Boom
versions.text:
The sky turns dark. Tall gray clouds roll in. A storm is on its way.

Then there is a bright flash. That is lightning. Lightning is a huge spark. It is made of electricity.

How does it start? A storm cloud is full of bits of ice and drops of rain. The wind tosses them up and down. They bump and rub. This builds up a charge in the cloud. When the charge gets too big, a giant spark jumps. It can jump inside the cloud. It can also jump down to the ground.

The spark is very hot. It is hotter than the top of the sun! It heats the air in a flash. The hot air pushes out fast. That makes a loud boom. The boom is thunder.

We see the flash first. Then we hear the boom. That is because light moves fast, and sound is slow. Count the seconds from the flash to the boom. Three seconds means the storm is about one kilometer away.

What should you do in a storm? Go inside. Find a safe shelter, like a house or a car. Do not stand by a tall tree. Stay out of the water. Wait half an hour after the last boom. Then it is safe to go out.

The flash is lightning. Lightning is a giant spark of electricity. Have you felt a tiny spark when you touch a door handle? Lightning is like that, but much, much bigger.

How does lightning start? A storm cloud is full of tiny bits of ice and drops of water. Strong winds toss them up and down. They bump and rub against each other. This builds up an electric charge in the cloud. When the charge gets too big, a huge spark jumps. It can jump inside the cloud or down to the ground.

Lightning is very hot. It is about five times hotter than the top of the sun! It heats the air in a split second. The hot air pushes out very fast and makes a loud boom. That boom is thunder.

We see the flash before we hear the thunder. This is because light moves much faster than sound. Count the seconds between the flash and the boom. Every three seconds means the storm is about one kilometer away.

Lightning can be dangerous. When you hear thunder, go inside a house or a car. These are safe shelters. Stay away from tall trees, open fields, and water. Wait thirty minutes after the last boom before you go back out.

versions.title: Lightning and Thunder
versions.text:
Dark clouds pile up high in the sky. The air feels heavy. A storm is coming. Suddenly, a bright flash zigzags across the sky. A few seconds later, a loud boom shakes the windows.

That flash is lightning. It is a giant spark of electricity. Have you ever touched a metal door handle and felt a tiny shock? Lightning works in a similar way, but it is millions of times stronger.

Lightning begins inside tall storm clouds. These clouds are full of tiny pieces of ice and drops of water. Strong winds push them up and down. They bump and rub against each other. This builds up an electric charge. The bottom of the cloud usually becomes negative, and the top becomes positive. When the charge gets too strong, a giant spark jumps. It can flash inside the cloud, between two clouds, or down to the ground.

A bolt of lightning is about five times hotter than the surface of the sun. It heats the air around it in a split second. The hot air expands so quickly that it makes a loud boom. That boom is thunder.

We always see the flash before we hear the thunder, because light travels much faster than sound. Count the seconds between them. Every three seconds means the storm is about one kilometer away.

Lightning can be very dangerous. When you hear thunder, go inside a building or a car right away. These make safe shelters. Stay away from tall trees, open fields, and water. Wait thirty minutes after the last thunder before going back outside.

versions.title: Lightning and Thunder
versions.text:
The air feels heavy, and dark clouds tower high above the land. Suddenly, a jagged flash splits the sky, and a few seconds later a deep boom shakes the windows. You have just seen lightning and heard thunder, two parts of the same powerful event.

Lightning is a giant spark of electricity. You may have felt a tiny spark when you touched a metal door handle after walking across a carpet. Lightning works in a similar way, but it is millions of times stronger.

Lightning forms inside tall storm clouds. These clouds are full of tiny particles of ice and drops of water. Strong winds carry the particles up and down. They crash and rub against each other. As they do, they build up an electric charge. Usually, the bottom of the cloud gathers a negative charge, while the top gathers a positive charge. When the difference becomes too great, a huge spark jumps to balance it. The spark can flash inside a cloud, leap between clouds, or strike the ground.

A lightning bolt is about five times hotter than the surface of the sun. It heats the air around it in a fraction of a second. The hot air expands so fast that it creates a loud wave of sound. That sound is thunder.

We see lightning before we hear thunder because light travels much faster than sound. You can use this to estimate how far away a storm is. Count the seconds between the flash and the boom. Every three seconds equals about one kilometer.

Lightning is dangerous, so safety matters. When you hear thunder, go inside a building or a car. Stay away from tall trees, open fields, and water. Wait thirty minutes after the last thunder before going outside. Many tall buildings also have a lightning rod, a metal bar on the roof that guides lightning safely into the ground.

versions.text:
The atmosphere feels heavy and humid, and enormous dark clouds tower above the landscape. Suddenly, a jagged streak of brilliant light divides the sky, and several seconds later a deep rumble rattles the windows. You have just witnessed lightning and thunder, which are two connected parts of a single, remarkably powerful natural event.

Lightning is a gigantic electrical discharge, or a sudden release of stored electricity. You may have experienced a miniature version when you touched a metal door handle after walking across a carpet and felt an unexpected shock. Lightning operates according to the same principle, although it is millions of times more powerful.

Lightning develops inside towering thunderstorm clouds, which contain countless tiny particles of ice and droplets of water. Powerful currents of air carry these particles upward and downward, so they constantly collide and rub against each other, gradually separating electric charges. Typically, the lower portion of the cloud accumulates a negative charge, while the upper portion accumulates a positive charge. When the imbalance becomes too great for the air to resist, an enormous spark jumps to neutralize it. This discharge may flash within a single cloud, travel between separate clouds, or strike the ground.

It heats the surrounding air in a fraction of a second, and the air expands so violently that it produces a powerful shock wave. That shock wave reaches our ears as thunder.

We observe lightning before we hear thunder because light travels about a million times faster than sound. This difference allows you to estimate the distance to a storm. Count the seconds between the flash and the boom, since every three seconds corresponds to approximately one kilometer.

Because lightning is extremely dangerous, sensible precautions are essential. Whenever you hear thunder, move inside a building or an enclosed car immediately. Avoid tall trees, open fields, and water, which are particularly risky locations. Wait thirty minutes after the final thunder before returning outside. Many tall buildings are also protected by a lightning rod, a metal bar that acts as a conductor, guiding electricity safely into the ground. The American scientist Benjamin Franklin invented the lightning rod during the eighteenth century, and similar devices continue to protect buildings throughout the world today.

wrong.C: The article says lightning is about five times hotter than the sun's surface.

questions.stem: What separates the electric charges inside a thunderstorm cloud?
options: Sunlight shining on the top of the cloud
Lightning rods on tall buildings
Thunder shaking the cloud apart
Colliding ice particles and water droplets
questions.why: The article says vertical air currents carry ice and water particles up and down so they collide and separate charges.

wrong.A: Sunlight is not described as a cause.
wrong.B: Lightning rods protect buildings; they do not affect clouds.
wrong.C: Thunder comes after lightning; it does not create the charge.

questions.stem: Read: "an enormous spark jumps to neutralize it." What does neutralize mean in this sentence?
options: To make something louder
To cancel out or balance something
To freeze something solid
To make something grow stronger
questions.why: The spark releases the built-up imbalance between negative and positive charges, balancing them.

wrong.C: Nothing freezes; the spark is extremely hot.
wrong.D: The spark ends the imbalance; it does not strengthen it.

questions.stem: What directly produces the shock wave we hear as thunder?
options: Droplets of water striking the ground very hard during the heaviest part of the storm
Clouds moving apart at high speed
Charges forming at the top of the cloud
Air expanding explosively after it is suddenly heated
questions.why: The article says the bolt heats the air in a fraction of a second, so the air expands explosively and creates a shock wave.

wrong.A: Rain is not the cause of thunder.
wrong.B: The article does not describe clouds separating.
wrong.C: Charges build before the strike; the shock wave comes from heated air.

questions.stem: The article says the spark jumps when the imbalance is "too great for the surrounding air to resist." What can you infer about air?
options: Air usually blocks electricity until the charge becomes very strong.
Air is a perfect conductor of electricity.
Air has no effect on lightning at all.
Air makes the charge inside clouds.
questions.why: If the air must be overcome, it normally resists the flow of electricity until the charge builds up enough.

wrong.B: If air conducted easily, charge could not build up so much.
wrong.C: The phrase shows the air does resist for a while.
wrong.D: Colliding particles make the charge, not the air.

questions.stem: Omar counts nine seconds between a flash and its thunder and decides the storm is too far to matter. Based on the article, why is he wrong?
options: Nine seconds means the storm is already gone.
Thunder can only be heard when lightning strikes very near the person listening.
The storm is about three kilometers away, so he should take shelter.
Light and sound arrive at the same time, so he counted wrong.
questions.why: Every three seconds equals about one kilometer, and the article says to move indoors whenever thunder is audible.

wrong.A: Thunder shows the storm is still active.
wrong.B: Thunder can be heard from far away.
wrong.D: Light travels much faster than sound.

questions.stem: How is the article mainly organized?
options: It lists storms in order of size.
It explains how lightning forms and causes thunder, then gives safety advice.
It tells the life story of Benjamin Franklin from his childhood to his old age.
It compares storms in different countries.
questions.why: The article moves from definition, to cause, to effects, and ends with precautions.

wrong.A: No list of storms is given.
wrong.C: Franklin appears only near the end.
wrong.D: The article does not compare countries.

HIGH.prompt: A classmate says, "Thunder can't hurt you, so it is safe to stay outside until the lightning is right overhead." Write a response that uses scientific facts from the article to explain why this idea is dangerous.
checklist: I clearly explained why the classmate's idea is wrong.
I used at least three scientific facts from the article, such as how distance is estimated or how lightning forms.
I organized my response with a clear opening, supporting reasons, and a conclusion.
